# Project Display-Test Equipment Operating Basis

## Purpose and authority

This document is a sanitized operating extract from the project's approved internal SOP. It describes the available test-chain roles and reusable operating controls. It deliberately omits the project's test-item catalog, case identifiers, case-to-procedure mapping, acceptance values, expected results, and report examples.

The project SOP, rather than the supplied R&S SMW200A manufacturer guide, is the authority for the project display-test workflow. Similar equipment names must not be treated as interchangeable.

## Equipment roles

- The project test chain includes an HDMI 2.1 signal source capable of supplying the HDR formats needed by the approved test plan.
- The project uses an SNW200A all-in-one display tester with brightness-meter, colorimeter, and oscilloscope functions.
- A brightness-meter or colorimeter probe may be positioned at the prescribed screen measurement location and must be calibrated before measurement.
- The project control software exposes connection status and measurement or recording functions used by the approved procedure.
- The exact routing between the signal source, display tester, probe, and television must be verified from the installed test-chain configuration before a measurement-dependent test is accepted.

## Reusable operating sequence

1. Verify the HDMI path, selected television input, cable suitability, and source-to-display connection.
2. Power and warm the test equipment and television according to the approved preparation requirements.
3. Calibrate or zero the applicable optical probe and confirm that the control software reports the required devices as connected.
4. Configure the signal source for the required HDR format, timing, bit depth, metadata, and test pattern supported by the selected test objective.
5. Configure the display tester for the required observation, brightness measurement, color measurement, high-frequency sampling, or time-based recording operation.
6. Apply the stimulus, confirm the intended television mode or signal state, and perform the planned observation or measurement.
7. Record source settings, television settings, measurement conditions, readings, transition timing, visible artifacts, and any signal-chain exception needed to interpret the result.

## Control rules

- Do not infer SNW200A interfaces, commands, or capabilities from the R&S SMW200A guide.
- Do not assign one instrument every role merely because the project workflow uses several components together.
- A measurement-dependent result is invalid when the signal path, probe calibration, or software connection has not been verified.
- Use only the acceptance relationship supplied by the project's final approved requirements; do not recover superseded values from historical SOP versions.
- When a requested setting is not established by the supplied evidence, state the required function or controlled condition without inventing a button name, port label, sampling value, software command, or instrument feature.

LG OLED65C22LB
HDR Acceptance Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)
Acceptance Requirements Reference

1. Document Information
2. Pre-Test Preparation and Environmental Requirements
2.1 Environmental Conditions
• Dark room requirement: Ambient illuminance ≤ 0.3 lx (OLED is extremely sensitive to stray light; full darkness required)
• Temperature & Humidity: 25±3℃, relative humidity 25%-85%, avoid condensation
• Test HDMI Cable: Must use certified HDMI 2.1 cable
2.2 Instrument Warm-up and Calibration
• SNW200A instrument warm-up ≥ 30 seconds; confirm panel indicator is solid green
• Brightness meter/colorimeter probe must complete zero calibration (Calibrate) before measurement
• Confirm device status shows "Connected" in software
2.3 Screen Settings
• Disable auto brightness, eye care mode, and power saving mode
• Select corresponding picture mode based on test item (Standard / Dynamic / Cinema / Filmmaker Mode / HDR10 Pro / Dolby Vision / HLG / Game Optimizer)
• Set brightness/contrast to factory default or test requirement value
• Ensure TV has been warmed up for at least 30 minutes, with brightness change rate < 2%/min
• Enable Brightness Booster / Dynamic Tone Mapping Pro and other functions as needed for testing
3. Acceptance Decision Rules
3.1 Pass Criteria
• When all applicable acceptance requirements pass, the HDR acceptance is deemed qualified.
• When any single item fails (Fail), record specific deviation values and phenomena, assess whether it affects actual user experience
• If signal-chain verification fails, measurement-dependent checks are invalid until the connection issue is resolved.
3.2 Project-Specific Acceptance Parameters
4. Precautions and Troubleshooting Guide

PAGE 1
HDR Technology - Complete Specification Guide (Part 1)
Section 1: General HDR Technology Overview
Chapter 1: Introduction to HDR
What is HDR (High Dynamic Range)
High Dynamic Range (HDR) significantly expands both the contrast ratio and color 
gamut compared to Standard Dynamic Range (SDR). It captures and displays a much 
wider range of luminance levels, from the deepest blacks to the brightest highlights, 
reproducing images that are closer to human visual perception.
Evolution from SDR to HDR
SDR is traditionally limited to an 8-bit color depth (16.7 million colors), the Rec.709 
color gamut (covering approximately 36% of Rec.2020), and a peak brightness of 
around 100 nits. HDR transcends these limitations by introducing 10-bit or higher 
color depth, the Rec.2020 color gamut, and peak brightness capabilities reaching up 
to 10,000 nits.
Core Advantages
• Wider Contrast Ratio: Up to 1,000,000:1 compared to 1,000:1 for SDR.
• Expanded Color Gamut: Utilizes Rec.2020 versus the legacy Rec.709.
• Higher Peak Brightness: Ranges from 1,000 to 10,000 nits versus 100 nits for SDR.
• Increased Color Depth: Supports 10-bit+ color depth (1.07 billion+ colors) versus 
16.7 million colors.
• Improved Detail: Superior retention of detail in both highlights and shadows.

Chapter 2: HDR Signal Formats Overview
• HDR10: Utilizes static metadata, 10-bit color depth, up to 10,000 nits, and 
Rec.2020 color gamut. It uses the SMPTE ST 2084 (PQ) EOTF. As an open and 
royalty-free format, it is the most universally supported HDR standard.
• HDR10+: Features dynamic metadata at the frame or scene level, supporting 
10/12-bit color, up to 10,000 nits, and Rec.2020. It uses the SMPTE ST 2084 EOTF. 
Developed by Samsung, Panasonic, and 20th Century Fox, it is open, royalty-free, 
and backward compatible with HDR10.

PAGE 2
• Dolby Vision: Employs dynamic metadata on a per-frame basis, supporting up to 
12-bit color, up to 10,000 nits, and Rec.2020. It uses the PQ EOTF. This is a 
proprietary, paid licensing format with specific profiles (5/7/8/10) and per-frame 
tone mapping.
• HLG (Hybrid Log-Gamma): Contains no external metadata (metadata is inherent 
in the signal). It supports 10-bit color, up to 1,000 nits reference brightness, and 
Rec.2020. Using the Hybrid Log-Gamma EOTF, it is open, royalty-free, developed 
by BBC R&D and NHK, broadcast-compatible, and fully SDR backward 
compatible.
• HDR Vivid: Features per-frame dynamic metadata, 10/12-bit color, up to 10,000 
nits, and Rec.2020. It uses the PQ EOTF and an open licensing model by CAIA. 
Focused on the Chinese market, it utilizes a Smart Tone Mapping algorithm.

Chapter 4: Core Hardware Parameters
• Peak Brightness: Determines highlight performance. ≥600 nits is required for a 
noticeable HDR improvement, while high-end displays target ≥1000 nits.
• Contrast Ratio: High-end HDR requires ≥10,000:1. OLED technology can reach 
million-to-one contrast ratios.

PAGE 4
• Color Depth: 8-bit provides 16.7M colors (prone to banding); 10-bit provides 1.07B 
colors (HDR standard); 12-bit provides 68.7B colors (used in Dolby Vision).
• Color Gamut: BT.709 is used for SDR (~36% of Rec.2020); DCI-P3 is used for digital 
cinema (~75% of Rec.2020); Rec.2020 is the ultra-wide HDR standard (current 
displays achieve 70-90% coverage).
• Local Dimming: Global dims the entire backlight; 1D/1.5D dims vertical or 
horizontal zones; 2D (Full Array) offers the best performance.
• EOTF (Electro-Optical Transfer Function): PQ (SMPTE ST 2084) maps to absolute 
luminance; HLG (Hybrid Log-Gamma) is broadcast-friendly.
Chapter 5: HDR Tone Mapping
• What is Tone Mapping: The process of adapting HDR content to a display’s 
specific capabilities by mapping source luminance to the display’s luminance 
range.
• Static Tone Mapping: Uses global metadata (MaxCLL/MaxFALL) to apply a single 
tone curve for the entire content. Used by HDR10.
• Dynamic Tone Mapping: Uses per-frame or per-scene metadata to continuously 
optimize tone mapping. Used by HDR10+, Dolby Vision, and HDR Vivid.
• Tone Mapping Artifacts: Include clipping (lost highlight detail), crushing (lost 
shadow detail), banding (visible color steps), and halo effects (local dimming 
artifacts).
• Impact on Image Quality: Superior tone mapping preserves highlight detail, 
maintains shadow contrast, and ensures smooth color transitions.
Chapter 6: Testing Methodology (General)
Software/System-Level Testing
• EDID/HDR Capability Detection: Verify the receiver correctly parses sink EDID 
for HDR support, MaxCLL/MaxFALL, and colorimetry.
• Metadata Parsing: Validate that the SoC correctly extracts metadata from the 
stream.
• UI State Verification: Ensure OSD menus correctly reflect HDR mode and UI 
overlays are tone-mapped appropriately.
• Auto Switching: Verify seamless transitions between SDR and HDR modes.
Hardware/Quality Testing
• Photometric Measurements: Use spectroradiometers to measure peak 
brightness, black levels, and ANSI contrast.
• Colorimetry: Measure DCI-P3/Rec.2020 coverage and Delta E accuracy.
• Tone Mapping Accuracy: Verify EOTF matches specification within tolerance.
• Required Equipment: Calibrated spectroradiometer, HDR signal generator, 
reference monitor, HDMI protocol analyzer.
• Test Environment: Dark room (ambient light <1 lux) with a reference display for 
comparison.
Chapter 7: Industry Standards
• ITU-R BT.2100: Foundational HDR standard defining PQ and HLG EOTFs, 
Rec.2020 colorimetry, and 10/12-bit signals for 4K/8K.

PAGE 5
• SMPTE ST 2084: Defines the Perceptual Quantizer (PQ) EOTF, mapping code 
values to absolute luminance (0.0001 to 10,000 cd/m²).
• CEA-861.3: Specifies HDMI vendor-specific infoframes for HDR static and 
dynamic metadata transport.
• ITU-R BT.2446: Defines reference rendering conditions and conversion methods 
between HDR formats.
• ARIB STD-B67: Original HLG specification from ARIB (Japan).
• EBU R 111: European broadcasting recommendation for HLG.
Chapter 8: Appendix
Glossary of HDR Terms
• ABL: Auto Brightness Limiter
• EOTF: Electro-Optical Transfer Function
• MaxCLL: Maximum Content Light Level
• MaxFALL: Maximum Frame-Average Light Level
• PQ: Perceptual Quantizer
• HLG: Hybrid Log-Gamma
• Tone Mapping: Luminance adaptation process
• LLL: Logo Luminance Limiting
• Pixel Dimming: Individual pixel control (OLED)
• Burn-In: Permanent image retention
• Banding: Visible color stepping
• CEC: Consumer Electronics Control
• EDID: Extended Display Identification Data
• SEI: Supplemental Enhancement Information
• MDCV: Mastering Display Color Volume
• VSIF: Vendor-Specific InfoFrame
Recommended Test Content Sources
• Spears & Munsil UHD HDR Benchmark
• Disney+/Netflix Calibration Streams
• Light Illusion BPG Patterns
• VESA DisplayHDR Test App
Section 2: HDR10+ Technical Specification
Chapter 1: Introduction to HDR10+
• Overview: HDR10+ is an open, royalty-free HDR video format providing superior 
picture quality through dynamic metadata. It was developed by Samsung 
Electronics, Panasonic, and 20th Century Fox, and is governed by HDR10+ 
Technologies LLC (formerly HDR10+ Alliance).
• Key Differentiator vs HDR10: While HDR10 uses static metadata (one tone curve 
for entire content), HDR10+ uses dynamic metadata for per-frame or per-scene 
tone mapping adjustments, optimizing image quality dynamically.

PAGE 6
• Market Adoption: Supported by Samsung TVs, Amazon Prime Video, Disney+, 
Apple TV (via app), Panasonic, and various streaming platforms. It is also gaining 
traction in smart displays and satellite TV receivers.
Chapter 2: Technical Architecture
• Metadata Structure: HDR10+ dynamic metadata is structured for granular image 
control at two levels: Scene-level (applied to continuous frames with similar 
luminance) and Frame-level (applied to every individual frame for highest 
precision).
• Metadata Format: Based on SMPTE ST 2094-40 (Application 40) for dynamic 
metadata and SMPTE ST 2094-42 (Application 42) for extended metadata. MDCV 
(Maximum Content Display Volume) provides display characteristics.
• MDCV (Maximum Content Display Volume): Defines the maximum luminance 
and color volume the display can reproduce, enabling precise tone mapping.
• MaxCLL/MaxFALL: Maintains backward compatibility with HDR10 static 
metadata for legacy device support.
• Backward Compatibility: HDR10+ content falls back to HDR10 (static metadata) 
on devices that do not support HDR10+, ensuring universal playback.
Chapter 3: Signal Format & Transmission
• Signal Flow: Mastering suite (metadata generation) → Encoding/Transcoding → 
Distribution (broadcast/streaming/disc) → Receiver/SoC (metadata parsing) → 
Display (EOTF application and tone mapping).
• Metadata Injection Workflow: Offline grading with professional software 
(DaVinci Resolve, Baselight), automated or manual generation of SMPTE ST 
2094-40/42 metadata, injection into HEVC/AV1 SEI NAL units, and delivery via 
streaming/broadcast/physical media.
• HDMI Requirements: HDMI 2.0a minimum for 4K@60Hz HDR10+; HDMI 2.1 
required for 4K@120Hz and 8K. HDCP 2.2 is required for protected content.
• Bandwidth Analysis: 4K@60Hz HDR10+ typically requires 15-25 Mbps for 
streaming. Uncompressed 4K@120Hz requires HDMI 2.1 bandwidth (48 Gbps).
• Container Support: HEVC/H.265, AV1, H.264 (limited), VVC/H.266 (future).
Chapter 4: Core Specifications
• Color Depth: 10-bit (primary, mandatory); 12-bit (supported for future-proofing 
per SMPTE ST 2094-40).
• Color Gamut: Rec.2020/BT.2020 (mandatory WCG).
• Peak Brightness: Up to 10,000 nits mastering; displays map to native peak 
brightness.
• EOTF: SMPTE ST 2084 (PQ) primary; HLG supported.
• Resolution: Up to 8K UHD (7680x4320).
• Frame Rates: Up to 120fps.
• Chroma Subsampling: 4:4:4, 4:2:2, 4:2:0.

• HDR10+ vs Dolby Vision: Both use dynamic metadata, but Dolby Vision uses per-

requires paid licensing, whereas HDR10+ is free.
• HDR10+ vs HDR10: HDR10+ uses dynamic metadata versus HDR10′s static

Chapter 6: On OLED Displays
• OLED-Specific HDR10+ Behavior: Includes Pixel Dimming, ABL (Auto Brightness 
Limiter) interaction, LLL (Logo Luminance Limiting), and CEC mode switching.
• ABL Interaction: ABL reduces overall panel brightness for large bright areas. 
HDR10+ dynamic metadata provides precise luminance distribution info for 
smarter ABL algorithms, maintaining contrast and color saturation.
• LLL: Prevents burn-in by limiting static logo/border brightness. HDR10+ metadata 
helps balance LLL with HDR impact.
• CEC: HDR10+ mode changes can trigger CEC messages for automatic display/
input switching.
Chapter 7: Testing Methodology
• Software/System-Level Testing: EDID/HDR capability detection, metadata 
parsing (SMPTE ST 2094-40/42), UI state verification, auto switching between 
HDR10+ and HDR10, and compatibility testing across platforms (Netflix, YouTube, 
Apple TV+, gaming consoles).

PAGE 9
HDR Technology - Complete Specification Guide (Part 2)
Section 3: HDR10 Detailed Specification
Chapter 1: Introduction to HDR10
Overview and Origins HDR10 is the foundational HDR video format, established by 
the UHD Alliance in 2015. It serves as an open, royalty-free baseline standard for 
HDR content delivery. Championed by HDR10 LLC (now HDR Inc.), it is the most 
universally supported HDR format across satellite TV receivers, smart displays, 
streaming platforms, and physical media.
Core Standards Relationship The HDR10 specification is defined by two primary 
pillars: * SMPTE ST 2084 (PQ EOTF): The Perceptual Quantizer Electro-Optical 
Transfer Function replaces traditional gamma curves with absolute luminance 
mapping, supporting a range from 0.0001 to 10,000 cd/m². * ITU-R BT.2020 
(Rec.2020): Defines the wide color gamut (covering 125% of Rec.709) and supports 
10/12-bit color depth.
Use Cases HDR10 is utilized across a wide variety of platforms, including: * UHD Blu-
ray (mandatory HDR format) * Streaming services (Netflix, Amazon Prime, Disney+) * 
Broadcast standards (ATSC 3.0) * Gaming consoles and satellite TV receivers
Market Position As the universal baseline HDR format, HDR10 is required for all 
HDR-certified displays and remains the most widely supported format across devices 
and content platforms.
Chapter 2: Technical Architecture
Static Metadata Structure HDR10 utilizes static metadata embedded in the video 
bitstream via SEI (Supplemental Enhancement Information) messages in HEVC/
H.265 or VVC/H.266 codecs. For streaming or file delivery, this metadata is stored in 
container-level headers.
Metadata Parameters * MaxCLL (Maximum Content Light Level): Defines the 
brightest single pixel in the entire content. Displays use this to calibrate peak 
brightness. * MaxFALL (Maximum Frame-Average Light Level): Defines the 
brightest average frame in the content, used for overall brightness management. * 
MDCV (Mastering Display Color Volume): Optional per-content mastering display 
characteristics, including min/max luminance and color primaries.
Metadata Injection Workflow Colorists use professional grading software (e.g., 
DaVinci Resolve, Baselight) to analyze content and generate static metadata during 
the mastering phase. This metadata is then embedded into HEVC/AV1 SEI NAL units.
Backward Compatibility HDR10 signals are fully backward compatible with SDR 
displays through SDR-HDR conversion, utilizing Rec.2020 to BT.709 color space 
conversion and PQ to gamma EOTF conversion.
Chapter 3: Signal Format & Transmission
Signal Flow Mastering suite (metadata generation) → Encoding/Transcoding → 
Distribution (broadcast/streaming/disc) → Receiver/SoC (metadata parsing) → 
Display (EOTF application and tone mapping).

PAGE 10
HDMI Requirements * HDMI 2.0a: Minimum requirement for 4K@60Hz HDR10; 
requires HDCP 2.2 for protected content. * HDMI 2.1: Required for 4K@120Hz, 
8K@60Hz, and full 4:4:4 chroma subsampling at high frame rates.
Bandwidth Analysis * 4K@60Hz HDR10 typically requires 15–25 Mbps for streaming. 
* Uncompressed 4K@120Hz 10-bit 4:2:0 requires HDMI 2.1 bandwidth (48 Gbps). * 
8K@60Hz requires full HDMI 2.1 bandwidth.
Container Support Primary support is for HEVC/H.265, with H.264/AVC offering 
limited HDR10 support. VVC/H.266 is supported for future applications. Common 
containers include MP4, MKV, and TS for broadcast.

Section 4: Dolby Vision Technical Specification
Chapter 1: Introduction to Dolby Vision
Overview of Dolby Vision Technology Dolby Vision is a proprietary HDR video 
technology developed by Dolby Laboratories. It provides a comprehensive ecosystem 
for content creation, distribution, and playback, ensuring the creator’s original 
vision is accurately reproduced on consumer displays. Unlike standard HDR formats, 
Dolby Vision utilizes dynamic metadata to optimize image quality on a per-frame 
basis, providing the most precise tone mapping available in any HDR format.
Technology History Announced in 2014 with the first commercial product arriving 
in 2015, Dolby Vision was developed by Dolby Laboratories in partnership with major 
content creators (Netflix, Disney+, Apple TV+, Amazon Prime Video) and display 
manufacturers (LG OLED, Sony Bravia, Panasonic).
Certification Programs Dolby Vision certification is required for devices claiming 
support. It covers multiple profiles (5, 7, 8, 10) tailored for different use cases such as 
streaming, Blu-ray, and broadcast.
Market Position Dolby Vision is the premium HDR format used by major streaming 
platforms (Netflix, Disney+, Apple TV+, Amazon Prime Video), UHD Blu-ray, and 
high-end displays (LG OLED, Sony Bravia).
Chapter 2: Technical Architecture
Dynamic Metadata (Per-Frame) Dolby Vision calculates and applies maximum and 
average light levels for every single frame, enabling the most precise tone mapping 
available. This is more granular than HDR10+‘s scene-level or frame-level approach.
Mastering Display Metadata (MDCV) Per-frame MDCV provides display 
characteristics of the mastering monitor, including minimum and maximum 
luminance and color primaries, allowing the playback device to understand the 
content’s original intent.
Content Light Level Metadata While HDR10 uses static MaxCLL/MaxFALL, Dolby 
Vision calculates and applies per-frame maximum and average light levels, enabling 
highly accurate tone mapping and preventing clipping in bright scenes.

Dolby Vision Profiles * Profile 5: Streaming (SDR base layer + DV overlay, backward 
compatible with SDR) * Profile 7: Blu-ray (10-bit, 4:2:0, SDR base layer optional) * 
Profile 8: Streaming/Broadcast (10-bit, 4:2:2 or 4:4:4, no SDR base layer, most 
common for streaming) * Profile 10: Professional mastering (12-bit, 4:4:4, for content 
creation)
Comparison with HDR10 Metadata HDR10 uses static metadata (one set for entire 
content), whereas Dolby Vision uses per-frame dynamic metadata (unique set for 
every frame). Dolby Vision provides more precise tone mapping at the cost of higher 
processing overhead.

Encoding (Dolby Vision codec, e.g., dvhe.05, dvhe.08) → Distribution (streaming/
broadcast/disc) → Receiver/SoC (Dolby Vision profile negotiation, metadata parsing) 
→ Display (per-frame tone mapping).

encoding and an SDR base layer for backward compatibility. Dolby Vision video

based audio passthrough.

Section 5: HDR Vivid Technical Specification
Chapter 1: Introduction to HDR Vivid
Overview of HDR Vivid (菁彩影像)
HDR Vivid is a next-generation HDR video technology standard developed and 
promoted by the China Audio-Video Industry Association (CAIA). It is designed to 
deliver superior visual experiences through advanced dynamic metadata and 
intelligent tone mapping, ensuring that the creator’s original intent is accurately 
reproduced on consumer displays.
Development Background
HDR Vivid was developed in response to the need for a domestically-controlled HDR 
standard in China. It was initially published as the CAIA/T 0021-2021 standard and 
has since been incorporated into the national standard GB/T 46269.2-2025.
Key Differentiator: Smart Tone Mapping
The core differentiator of HDR Vivid is its Smart Tone Mapping (智能影调映射) 
algorithm. This algorithm uses per-frame dynamic metadata to optimize image 
quality in real-time, adapting seamlessly to specific display capabilities and viewing 
environments.
Market Adoption
HDR Vivid has achieved widespread adoption across the Chinese ecosystem: - 
Hardware: Supported by major smart TV manufacturers including Hisense, TCL, 
Skyworth, and Changhong. - Streaming: Integrated into platforms such as iQiyi, 
Tencent Video, Youku, and Mango TV. - Broadcast: Supported by China’s DTMB 
and ATSC 3.0 broadcast standards, as well as satellite TV receivers.
Chapter 2: Technical Architecture
Dynamic Metadata Structure
HDR Vivid utilizes per-frame dynamic metadata for granular image control. Each 
frame contains unique tone mapping parameters, including peak brightness, average 
brightness, and color volume information.
Per-Frame Tone Mapping Metadata
Unlike static metadata formats, HDR Vivid supports per-frame tone mapping 
metadata. This granular level of control ensures that rapid changes in scene lighting 
or color are accurately tracked, preventing clipping in bright highlights or crushing 
of shadow details during dynamic transitions.
Smart Tone Mapping Algorithm
The Smart Tone Mapping (智能影调映射) algorithm is the core of the HDR Vivid 
architecture. It analyzes content characteristics and display capabilities in real-time 
to optimize tone mapping by considering peak brightness, average luminance, and 
color volume, allowing the display to optimize rendering dynamically.

PAGE 18
Metadata Format & Compatibility
• Metadata Standard: Based on SMPTE ST 2094-40 (Application 40) for dynamic 
metadata, featuring CAIA-specific extensions for Smart Tone Mapping 
parameters.
• Backward Compatibility: HDR Vivid content can gracefully fall back to HDR10 or 
SDR on non-compatible displays through SDR-HDR conversion and static 
metadata mapping.
Chapter 3: Signal Format & Transmission
Signal Flow
1. Mastering Suite: HDR Vivid grading with reference monitor.
2. Encoding: CAIA codec, HEVC/AV1 with SEI metadata.
3. Distribution: Streaming, broadcast, or optical disc.
4. Receiver/SoC: HDR Vivid detection, metadata parsing, Smart Tone Mapping.
5. Display: Per-frame tone mapping execution.
HDMI & Bandwidth Requirements
• HDMI Version: HDMI 2.0 or higher is required. HDMI 2.1 is recommended for 
4K@120fps content to ensure sufficient bandwidth.
• Bandwidth Analysis: 4K@60fps with 10-bit 4:2:0 typically requires 20-40 Mbps for 
streaming. Uncompressed pass-through via HDMI 2.0 requires ~18 Gbps, while 
4K@120fps requires HDMI 2.1 bandwidth.
Container & Broadcast Support
• Containers: HEVC/H.265 (primary), AV1 (future), H.264 (limited), MP4, MKV, TS 
(broadcast).
• DTMB Support: Supported in China’s DTMB-2 broadcast standard for over-the-
air HDR transmission.
• ATSC 3.0 Support: Compatible with the ATSC 3.0 next-generation broadcast 
standard.
• Frame Rates & Subsampling: Supports up to 120fps and chroma subsampling of 
4:4:4, 4:2:2, and 4:2:0.

Section 6: HLG (Hybrid Log-Gamma) Technical Specification
Chapter 1: Introduction to HLG
HLG Technology Overview
Hybrid Log-Gamma (HLG) is an HDR video format jointly developed by BBC’s 
Research & Development (R&D) department in the UK and NHK (Japan Broadcasting 
Corporation). Designed to address unique challenges of live broadcasting, HLG has 
become a cornerstone of modern HDR transmission.
Broadcast-Friendly Design Philosophy
Unlike other HDR formats, HLG was designed specifically for live broadcasting 
where latency must be minimal and backward compatibility with SDR displays is 
essential. It requires no metadata, as HDR information is embedded directly in the 
signal.
Key Advantages for Broadcasting
• Zero Latency: No metadata processing overhead.
• Native SDR Backward Compatibility: SDR displays automatically render HLG 
content as SDR.

PAGE 23
• No Mastering Display Requirements: No need for reference monitors during 
production.
• Efficient Bandwidth Usage: Optimized for broadcast transmission.
Market Adoption
HLG is adopted by BBC (UK), NHK (Japan), Sky (UK), ESPN (USA), Eurosport, and 
various national broadcasters. It is the standard for ATSC 3.0 (USA), DVB (Europe), 
and ISDB (Japan/Brazil), widely used for live sports, news, and event broadcasting.
Chapter 2: Technical Architecture
Hybrid Log-Gamma EOTF
HLG combines two transfer functions: - Logarithmic Curve (Highlights): Efficiently 
encodes high dynamic range (up to 1000x to 10,000x relative to SDR peak brightness) 
in the highlight region. - Gamma Curve (Shadows/Midtones): Matches BT.1886 
gamma for SDR compatibility, ensuring SDR displays render HLG content with 
correct contrast.
Mathematical Formulation
The HLG EOTF is defined by a piecewise function: - For 0 <= V <= 1/a: E = (V/a)^gamma 
(Gamma curve for shadows/midtones) - For 1/a < V <= 1: E = (b * ln(V - c) + d) / e 
(Logarithmic curve for highlights) (Exact constants a, b, c, d, e, gamma are defined in 
ARIB STD-B67 and ITU-R BT.2100.)
“Inherent Metadata” Mechanism
HLG embeds display-referred information directly into the signal’s luminance 
levels, eliminating the need for separate metadata transmission. The signal is 
display-referred, meaning code values directly represent the intended luminance on 
the mastering display.
SDR Backward Compatibility & Mastering
SDR displays apply a built-in HLG-to-SDR conversion (using BT.1886 gamma curve), 
automatically rendering HLG content as properly exposed SDR without clipping or 
crushing. Furthermore, HLG does not require a calibrated reference monitor for 
content mastering; content can be created on standard SDR monitors with HLG-
aware grading tools.
Chapter 3: Signal Format & Transmission
Signal Structure & Broadcast Transmission
HLG signals consist of luminance (Y) and chrominance (Cb, Cr) components encoded 
with the HLG EOTF, requiring no separate metadata channel. - DVB: Supported in 
DVB-I and DVB-T2 standards. - ATSC 3.0: Mandatory HDR format for ATSC 3.0. - 
ISDB: Supported in ISDB-Tb (Japan/Brazil). - Streaming: Supported in HLS/MPEG-
DASH for OTT delivery.
HDMI & Bandwidth Requirements
• HDMI: HDMI 2.0a minimum for 4K@60Hz HLG. HDMI 2.1 required for 4K@120Hz 
and 8K. HDCP 2.2 required for protected content.

Format Comparisons & Recommendations
• HLG vs HDR10: HLG has no metadata (lower latency, broadcast-friendly) and is 
natively backward compatible with SDR. HDR10 uses static metadata and is better 
suited for recorded content.
• HLG vs Dolby Vision: HLG has zero latency (no metadata), making it ideal for live 
broadcasts. Dolby Vision uses per-frame metadata for superior quality but 
introduces higher latency, making it ideal for premium recorded content.
• Use Case Recommendations: HLG is mandatory for live broadcast and ATSC 3.0/
DVB/ISDB transmission. HDR10/HDR10+ is recommended for streaming and 
physical media. Dolby Vision is best for premium home theater, while HDR Vivid 
serves the Chinese market.
Chapter 6: On OLED Displays
OLED-Specific HLG Behavior
• Pixel Dimming Interaction: OLED pixel dimming algorithms must account for 
HLG’s logarithmic highlight encoding. Aggressive pixel dimming can cause 
visible artifacts in HLG’s log-encoded highlights.
• ABL Interaction: ABL reduces overall panel brightness for large bright areas. 
Because HLG is display-referred, OLED TVs must apply internal tone mapping to 
map the 1000-nit reference signal to the panel’s actual peak brightness.
• LLL (Logo Luminance Limiting): Prevents burn-in by limiting static logo/border 
brightness. HLG’s inherent metadata mechanism requires special handling for 
LLL on OLED panels.
• CEC & SDR Fallback: HLG mode detection can trigger CEC messages for 
automatic display/input switching. When displayed on SDR-only OLED panels, the 
display automatically applies HLG-to-SDR conversion (BT.1886 gamma), rendering 
content as properly exposed SDR without user intervention.
